# Localization & Marketing Strategy: Korean Slate, 2026

*(Figures are illustrative planning assumptions; the frameworks are the deliverable.)*

---

## 1. The Core Strategic Insight

Most platforms treat localization as a fulfillment cost applied uniformly by title. That is wrong on three counts:

1. **Dubbing is a demand lever, not a delivery format.** Its ROI varies 10x across market × genre × demographic. In dub-default markets (LatAm, Germany, Italy, and colloquial-Arabic melodrama audiences), the dub *is* the product. In Nordics, Netherlands, or Philippines urban cohorts, a dub adds cost and can actively repel the core viewer.
2. **A dub is a durable catalog asset, not a launch expense.** Correct evaluation is multi-year NPV of incremental viewing hours, retention, and acquisition — not opening-window performance. This flips the answer for evergreen romance and franchise IP versus topical, news-adjacent titles.
3. **Cost asymmetry defines the game.** Subtitling runs roughly $8–15/minute/language; quality dubbing $120–300/minute/language. A 16-episode drama subtitles into 35 languages for ~$400K but dubs into 8 languages for ~$1.8–2.5M. **Breadth is nearly free; depth is where the budget dies.** So: subtitle universally, dub surgically.

Strategy therefore = a **universal subtitle floor + a disciplined dubbing allocation engine + fandom-led marketing that treats transnational communities as one audience with local expressions.**

---

## 2. The Allocation Engine

### 2.1 Two-axis scoring

**Axis A — Title Travel & Durability Score (0–100)**

| Factor | Weight | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Genre dub-elasticity | 25 | Family melodrama, romance, historical epic = high. Sharp-edged thriller, workplace satire, youth comedy = lower |
| Cast/IP global recognition | 20 | K-pop cast, prior franchise, star director |
| Catalog longevity | 20 | Evergreen vs. topical (drives amortization period) |
| Narrative accessibility | 15 | Pace, plot density, dependence on wordplay/honorific nuance |
| Franchise potential | 10 | Justifies voice-continuity investment |
| Fandom pre-signal | 10 | Pre-release chatter, source-IP (webtoon) fandom size |

**Axis B — Market Dub-Dependency Index (0–100)** per language, built from: historical dub-vs-sub completion-rate delta, dub-market share of competing local content, age skew of the Korean-content audience, subtitle literacy/reading comfort, and dub cost per minute.

### 2.2 Four localization packages

| Package | Contents | Typical trigger |
|---|---|---|
| **P0 — Floor (all titles, all markets)** | Human-reviewed subtitles in 32–40 languages, SDH/CC, audio description in 6, localized metadata/artwork, glossary compliance | Universal. Non-negotiable |
| **P1 — Core Dub** | P0 + dub in LatAm Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese, colloquial Arabic, Thai, Bahasa Indonesia | Title score ≥ 55 |
| **P2 — Broad Dub** | P1 + German, French, Italian, Castilian Spanish, Tagalog, Vietnamese, Turkish, Hindi | Title score ≥ 75 |
| **P3 — Tentpole** | P2 + Polish, Japanese, Mandarin, additional SEA/Gulf dialects, day-and-date all-language dub, dub-cast press tour | Top 8–10 titles/yr |

Note the ordering: **LatAm Spanish and Brazilian Portuguese sit in the *first* dub tier ahead of German or French**, because dub-dependency is near-absolute, cost per minute is mid-range, and audience scale is large. Nordics, Netherlands, Portugal, Greece, and the anglophone markets stay subtitle-only at every tier — that single decision funds roughly two additional dub languages.

### 2.3 Sequencing as a marketing weapon

- **Day 1:** subtitles everywhere, globally simultaneous (piracy and fansub defense).
- **Day 1:** dubs live in P1 markets for any title scoring ≥55, and all P2/P3 languages for tentpoles.
- **Day +30/45:** "Dub Wave 2" for mid-tier titles — deliberately merchandised as a **second launch beat** with its own artwork, dub-cast content, and recommendation push. This converts a cost-saving delay into a free second window of promotional inventory, and lets Wave-2 language selection be *decided by Week-2 subtitle performance data* rather than guessed pre-launch.

---

## 3. Budget Allocation

**Illustrative envelope: $100M localization + localized marketing creative.**

| Line | Share | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| P0 subtitle floor + accessibility (whole slate) | $10M | Cheap breadth; the highest-ROI line in the budget |
| Tier A dubs (top 10 tentpoles, P3) | $34M | Concentrated bets where dub drives acquisition |
| Tier B dubs (next ~25 titles, P1/P2) | $15M | Volume layer, mostly Wave-2 sequenced |
| Market-specific dubs (Gulf/Levantine dialects, Vietnamese VO, Tagalog, regional SEA) | $8M | Small-ticket, high-signal local bets |
| Localized marketing creative & talent | $14M | Artwork, trailers, dub-cast content, creator programs |
| Cultural advisory, editorial governance, versioning QA | $5M | Insurance against a single global-scandal edit |
| Tooling: glossaries, TM, AI post-edit pipeline, voice-continuity DB | $4M | Compounding efficiency asset |
| **Rapid-Response Hit Fund (unallocated)** | **$10M** | The most important line |

**On the Hit Fund:** Korean breakout hits are unpredictable and the value window is ~3 weeks. Hold 10% uncommitted with a **72-hour greenlight protocol**: if a title exceeds a defined velocity threshold in subtitle-only markets, pre-negotiated standby capacity at partner studios converts to a 10-day emergency dub. Pre-buy the option (retainers), not the capacity. Most organizations lose more value by being slow to a hit than by mis-sizing the base plan.

**Governance:** stage-gate the Tier B pool. Commit 60% pre-launch, release 40% on Week-2 performance. Run a rolling 70/20/10 discipline — 70% proven allocations, 20% tested expansions (new language, new genre-dub pairing), 10% pure experiment.

---

## 4. Regional Playbooks

### Latin America — *Dub is table stakes; compete on dub quality*
- **Format:** Near-100% dub coverage for scripted. Neutral LatAm Spanish + Brazilian Portuguese, day-and-date.
- **Differentiator:** **Voice-continuity casting** — lock the same Spanish/Portuguese voice actor to the same Korean star across every title. Over 2–3 years this builds transferable star equity in the dub market and creates a marketing hook competitors can't replicate quickly. Budget it as talent investment, not per-project casting.
- **Sensitivities:** low friction on content; high sensitivity to *dub quality* (a bad dub becomes a meme within 48 hours).
- **Marketing:** telenovela-adjacency positioning for melodrama; dub actors as promotable talent; K-pop crossover concerts/OST; heavy TikTok creator seeding.

### Southeast Asia — *Cheapest dub economics, most fragmented demand*
- **Format:** Thai and Bahasa Indonesia dubs are high-yield (family/romance co-viewing, strong dub norms, low unit cost). Philippines: subtitle-first for urban/young cohorts, **Tagalog dub only for broad family titles**. Vietnam: use the low-cost *thuyết minh* voice-over convention as a middle tier before committing to full dub.
- **Sensitivities:** Indonesia and Malaysia — religious content, alcohol, LGBTQ depiction, regulatory review. Handle by **market versioning**, never global edits.
- **Marketing:** mobile-first vertical assets; telco bundling and low-price-tier alignment; local celebrity reaction/watch-along content; Ramadan and regional holiday calendars.

### Middle East & North Africa — *The dialect decision is the strategy*
- **Format:** MSA subtitles as the floor. But the region's proven demand engine is **colloquial-dialect dubbing of long-form melodrama** — the Turkish-drama playbook. Korean family/romance melodrama is the closest analogue in the catalog.
- **Test to run in Year 1:** Levantine vs. Khaliji dub of the same title, split by market, measured on completion and retention. This is the single highest-value experiment in the whole plan; resolve it before scaling Arabic dub spend.
- **Sensitivities:** highest of any region and *non-uniform* (Gulf regulatory vs. Levant/Maghreb). Compliance versions are legitimate; disguised global edits are not.
- **Marketing:** Ramadan windowing for family titles; Gulf-market premium positioning; Arabic-language fandom accounts are highly organized and cross-post to global fandom instantly.

### Europe — *Bifurcate hard and bank the savings*
- **Dub markets:** Germany, France, Italy, Spain (Castilian), Turkey — dub only titles scoring ≥75, because per-minute costs are the highest in the portfolio. Poland: default to *lektor* voice-over (a fraction of dub cost) except for family titles.
- **Subtitle-only markets:** Nordics, Netherlands, Portugal, Greece, UK/Ireland, Belgium. No dub investment. This is the plan's largest deliberate saving.
- **Emerging shift:** under-35 European cohorts have materially higher subtitle tolerance post-*Parasite*/*Squid Game*. Track dub-uptake share annually by age; where under-35 dub share falls below a threshold in a given market, downgrade that language's tier and redeploy the money.
- **Marketing:** critical/prestige framing, festival adjacency, arthouse press for auteur titles; dub-star casting announcements as a distinct news beat in DE/FR/IT.

---

## 5. Cultural Adaptation Policy

**Governing principle: transcreate, don't erase.** Korean specificity is the product's competitive advantage; sanding it off destroys the reason audiences chose it.

**Three-category edit taxonomy — every change must be classified:**

| Category | Rule |
|---|---|
| **1. Regulatory/compliance** | Permitted as a *labeled market version*. Logged in a version registry. Never applied globally |
| **2. Linguistic transcreation** (idiom, wordplay, honorifics, food/brand references) | Encouraged. Governed by a per-title glossary approved by the Korean production |
| **3. Narrative/thematic alteration** | **Prohibited without creator sign-off.** Contractually require consultation rights in content deals |

**Specific handling standards:**
- **Honorifics** (*oppa, sunbae, -ssi*, formal/informal registers): retain in subtitles for fandom-heavy languages; in dubs, encode hierarchy through vocal register and naming conventions rather than deleting it. Fandoms treat honorific erasure as a trust violation and will publicize it.
- **Historically sensitive content** (colonial period, Korean War, North Korea, chaebol/class critique, shamanism): route through a **Regional Cultural Advisory Panel** — paid external advisors, not staff — with a 48-hour SLA and a documented escalation path. Their role is risk-flagging and framing advice, not editing.
- **Context, not cuts:** where a reference won't land, add a supporting layer (in-player context cards, glossary microsite, creator explainer content) rather than rewriting dialogue.
- **Transparency by default:** disclose when a market version differs. Assume any discovered discrepancy goes global within 24 hours — because it will.

---

## 6. Fandom Strategy: One Transnational Audience, Many Local Expressions

Korean-content fandom is not a set of national audiences; it is a single networked community that shares subtitles, screenshots, and grievances across borders in real time. Design for that.

1. **Global day-and-date availability is the primary anti-piracy tool.** Every day of staggered release manufactures a fansub. Protect it even when it strains dub capacity — this is why Wave-2 dubbing (not staggered *release*) is the correct cost lever.
